title: Trustworthy, Context-Aware and Explainable AI
text:
The problem
Ontology-based context engineering brings together RDF/OWL knowledge graphs, data and claim provenance, SHACL validation, diagnostics of embedding spaces, rule-guided assembly of context and verifiable operation of LLMs and agents.
A further strand studies the interpretability of models through LLM-based reasoning about executable machine-learning models (for example PMML), validated by direct execution, together with sensitivity to the model and the prompt. In processes, pre-modelled BPMN and case-based CMMN logic can be compared with governed, agent-based workflows. The shared question: at which decision points is autonomy justified, what context is needed, and how can added value and error risk be measured?
For explainability, a technically verifiable model and an explanation that users understand are two different qualities. A plausible explanation can create unwarranted certainty, so we judge an explanation by whether it improves error detection and correct decisions – not merely satisfaction or trust. Comparing no explanation, an expert explanation and a lay explanation can be a psychological experiment in its own right.

title: Trustworthy, Context-Aware and Explainable AI
text:
Research questions


How can knowledge graphs, provenance and validation make the behavior of LLMs and agents checkable?
Can LLMs reliably interpret executable machine-learning models when their claims are validated by execution?
At which decision points is agent autonomy justified, and how are its added value and error risk measured?
Do explanations improve error detection and decisions – or only satisfaction and trust?

title: AI Risk, Governance and Responsible Autonomy
text:
The problem
The analysis covers technical failures (hallucination, bias, data quality, model change), human and social risks (over-reliance, loss of autonomy, exclusion, convergence, erosion of trust), organizational risks (responsibility gaps, concentration of knowledge, role conflicts) and societal and legal consequences. ISO/IEC 23894, the management-system logic of ISO/IEC 42001 and EU regulation serve as application frameworks; conformity is always assessed for a concrete use case and role. Persona-based and classical FMEA, incident analysis, scenario-based examination and human oversight points can be combined – and the effectiveness of the responses to risks has to be measured too.
We measure self-reported trust, the actual acceptance of suggestions and checking behavior separately. A typical experimental question: does the user notice a convincingly worded error? A further question is which roles, competences and HR development AI governance requires as an organization matures, and how the uncertainty of a decision can tell when a system may act on its own and when a person has to be involved – the human-in-the-loop threshold.
Human oversight has psychological preconditions. Involving a person is meaningful control only if the overseer has the knowledge, time, access and right to override the system; the presence of a designated overseer does not in itself prove that oversight works. We study sustained attention, understanding of the rationale, recognizing when to escalate and the experience of decision responsibility; proposed outcomes are the detection rate of wrong suggestions and the time to a correct intervention.

title: AI Risk, Governance and Responsible Autonomy
text:
Research questions


How can risk be assessed across technical, human, organizational and societal layers for a concrete use case?
What reliance is appropriate for a given system and task, and how can it be measured beyond self-reported trust?
When may a system decide on its own and when must a person be involved – can this threshold be derived from decision uncertainty?
What roles, competences and HR development does AI governance require as organizations mature?
Under which conditions is human oversight effective rather than nominal?

title: Cognitive Partnership, Creativity and Relationships
text:
The problem
Working with AI can raise performance and support learning – and it can also weaken critical checking, one’s own initiative and the effort people invest in relationships. Availability, personalization, affirming communication and anthropomorphism all play a part. Within competence we measure three things separately: actual knowledge, perceived competence and task-specific self-efficacy. Someone may achieve more with AI and yet feel the success is less their own; the opposite risk, overconfidence, matters just as much.
The tension between individual productivity and collective homogenization is a particularly promising direction. Ideas suggested by AI can improve individual work while making the works of different people more alike. We therefore measure the novelty, usefulness and mutual distinctness of ideas separately, compare an “own idea first, AI second” sequence with the reverse, and extend the question to longer learning periods and group creativity.
“The digital self” covers several different phenomena: online self-presentation, the digitally extended self, AI-supported interpretation of one’s own life story, and agents acting in our name. The “AI cocoon” is a useful working idea but not yet an established construct; we phrase it as a question – after using AI, do people turn to each other more or less easily? – and study it longitudinally. Simulated societies of LLM agents can illuminate mechanisms, but conclusions about human groups require external validation with real participants.

title: Cognitive Partnership, Creativity and Relationships
text:
Research questions


When does working with AI improve performance and learning, and when does it weaken critical checking, own initiative and relational activity?
How do actual knowledge, perceived competence and self-efficacy diverge when people work with AI?
Does AI raise individual creativity while narrowing collective diversity – and does the order of own ideas and AI ideas matter?
How do personal address, signals of memory and empathic-sounding replies influence feeling understood, self-disclosure and judgments of reliability?
After using AI, do people turn to each other more or less easily – and for whom?

title: Building AI Capability in Enterprises and SMEs
text:
The problem
SMEs show every level of our framework at once: individual competence, collaboration in small teams, organizational learning and the digital divide between enterprises. The AI literacy and deployer obligations of the EU AI Act affect SMEs as well.
The line builds on an AI-maturity survey of SMEs covering five dimensions – strategy and leadership, data and infrastructure, skills and culture, AI applications, governance and ethics – with immediate feedback and analysis linked to company data, and on practical guides that show AI applications such as AI-supported quotation, virtual assistants and the early signalling of liquidity problems.

title: Building AI Capability in Enterprises and SMEs
text:
Research questions


What drives the development of SMEs’ AI capability – leadership intent, data and skills, or employees’ trust and sense of competence?
How does work change in a small enterprise after AI is introduced: which routine tasks disappear, and which new checking and learning demands appear?
Does a maturity diagnosis with targeted feedback change practice, and what turns a productivity guide into lasting change?
How can AI support generational succession – the transfer of an experienced owner’s tacit knowledge – while trust and roles are also renegotiated?
How large is the gap in AI capability between enterprises, where does it arise, and which policy instruments reduce it?

Foundations at the University of Pannonia

The Faculty of Business and Economics brings management, knowledge-management and quantitative research; the Faculty of Engineering contributes digital-transformation and maturity-assessment experience; student teams can work on real SME challenges through student research, theses and doctoral pre-studies.

title: Building AI Capability in Enterprises and SMEs

H10 In small and medium-sized enterprises, an AI-maturity diagnosis with targeted feedback leads to lasting change in practice if adoption is also supported by employees’ sense of competence and trust.

title: About the network
text:
Why now
The most rigorous recent studies show that the effect of AI on people is not automatically positive: design, context and expertise decide its sign. In field experiments, AI assistance raised productivity most for less experienced workers, and helped professionals from different backgrounds reach similar solutions; unrestricted access to a chatbot improved students’ practice performance but harmed their later independent performance, while a tutor designed for learning largely removed the harm; and greater trust in generative AI went together with less critical thinking among knowledge workers. Organizations adopt AI faster than these effects are understood.
Regulation raises the stakes. The EU AI Act treats AI systems used in education and employment as high-risk and prohibits emotion recognition in schools and workplaces; ISO/IEC 42001 defines a certifiable AI management system. Universities are expected to show measurable preparedness – in their own operation as well as in research. The University’s institutional development plan for 2026–2030 names the human-centered AI university as a guiding principle; the network is its research leg, producing knowledge for the University’s own AI deployment and sharing it with the region.

title: About the network
text:
How the network works
The network is open, cross-faculty and self-organizing. Members keep their institutional and project affiliations and connect around shared research questions, data and methodological infrastructure, publications and pilots. The Network of Research Excellence provides visibility, a meeting point and light coordination; no separate organizational unit, new hierarchy or large dedicated budget is needed to start.
A coordinator and voluntary topic leads support the collaboration. Contributions and authorship are agreed in advance according to transparent principles. The network’s formats – a monthly open research forum, a research clinic every two months and an annual doctoral day – are described under Activities. Doctoral research runs in the existing doctoral schools, with a shared layer on top.
What counts as success follows from the nature of research rather than from an administrative calendar: new multidisciplinary questions, results that genuinely connect researchers from several faculties, independently validated methods, citable publications, open research artifacts and documented institutional or social impact. Interdisciplinary work is known to be more visible but often less productive in the short term; recognizing it in developmental, CoARA-aligned research assessment is a condition for the network’s sustainability.

title: About the network
text:
International context
Before designing the network, we looked at how leading human-centered AI initiatives are organized, how they involve doctoral candidates and how they are funded. Several lessons shaped our model.



Initiative
What we take from it




Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI
Small, interdisciplinary seed support with an ethics and society review before funding; no separate PhD programme.


Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI
“First a network, then an institute”: the institute grew out of a university-wide network.


TU Delft AI Labs
Cross-faculty labs led jointly by researchers from two faculties; doctoral candidates co-supervised across disciplines.


Utrecht University – Human-centered AI
A virtual focus area with a simple rule: every group involves several faculties.


WASP-HS
A shared graduate-school layer instead of a new doctoral school.


Hybrid Intelligence Centre
A capability-based research framework and a conference series of its own (HHAI).


University of Aberdeen – Interdisciplinary Human-Centred AI Research Network
A minimal starting form: a light network with co-leads, lightning talks and events aligned with funding calls.


ELLIS
Joining an existing European network is cheaper than building a parallel structure; the degree stays at home, with a co-supervisor abroad.


MPIB Center for Humans and Machines
Large-sample online behavioral experiments on how people and machines interact.

Name and affiliation
The network’s name is Human- and Society-Centered AI Research Network, always used together with the University: “Human- and Society-Centered AI Research Network, University of Pannonia”. “Network” expresses the cross-faculty way of working without a separate organizational unit.

Our integrative unit of analysis is the human–AI–social system. AI outputs can redistribute attention, knowledge, responsibility, organizational roles, influence and risks – and they feed back into which systems are developed and deployed in the next cycle. Within this unit we keep three things apart: the operational autonomy of the AI, the intentionality people perceive in it, and human responsibility. How attributing agency to AI changes trust and the attribution of responsibility is itself a research question.

title: Approach
text:
A shared causal logic
The studies of the network are organized around five connected, empirically testable elements. Select an element to read about it.

  
  
  Use the mouse, or Tab and the arrow keys, then Enter.

The same application can increase individual productivity while homogenizing collective thinking; it can support independent decisions while creating over-reliance; it can ease the flow of knowledge in an organization while threatening professional identity. Uncovering and measuring these mechanisms, and drawing their design consequences, is the central task of the programme.

title: Approach
text:
Four connected levels
Mediating mechanisms belong to different levels of analysis. Cognitive load is typically measured at the person–task level; psychological safety can be a group characteristic if the conditions for aggregation hold; trust can be directed at the AI, at leadership or at colleagues. For every pilot we therefore fix in advance whether a concept is a precondition, mediator, moderator or outcome.

  
  
  Select a level – from the individual at the centre to society at the edge.

title: Approach
section: Human agency as the common thread
text:
Human agency as the common thread
The levels are connected by one question: preserving human agency. When does AI become help after which people can do more on their own, and when does the performance gain stay tied to the system? Self-determination theory, with its three basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence and relatedness – serves as a linking framework: we ask whether the use of AI supports these needs, and under which designs it frustrates them.

  Supported performancemeasured with AI
  Durable competencemeasured later, without AI, including transfer
  Independent initiativewhat people start, check and decide themselves

title: Approach
text:
Shared measurement principles


Actual and perceived apart. Actual knowledge, perceived competence and self-efficacy – and trust and actual reliance – are measured separately.
Self-report and behavior. Alongside self-reports we collect behavioral indicators: acceptance, checking, error detection, help-seeking.
Supported and independent performance. Performance is measured with AI and, with a delay, without it, to capture durable competence and transfer.
Level of analysis. We fix in advance whether a variable is individual, group or organizational, and when it may be aggregated.
The role of a concept. For each pilot we record whether a variable is a precondition, mediator, moderator or outcome.
Conceptual caution. Working concepts (such as the “AI cocoon”) are not treated as established constructs, and measuring a new concept is not replaced by renaming an existing scale.

title: Approach
text:
Methods
The University of Pannonia has internationally strong methodological foundations: complex networks and hypergraphs; possibilistic and fuzzy handling of uncertainty that distinguishes conflict from ignorance at the point of decision; simulation of LLM agents and agent societies; explainable machine learning; discrete-event simulation and digital twins. Because many of our questions are psychological, these are complemented by behavioral experiments, diary and longitudinal studies, the critical incident technique, qualitative interviews and multilevel analysis – not as a later check on technological results, but from the definition of the problem and the testing of alternative explanations onwards.

title: Approach
text:
Responsible research
Studies with data on students, employees or other people require a clarified legal basis, institutional approval, research-ethics clearance, access rules and data minimization in advance. No automatic personnel evaluation or ranking may be derived from the operation of the AI systems we study. The EU’s approach to trustworthy, human-centric AI and the risk-based logic of the AI Act provide the normative reference points; hypotheses come with controls, outcomes fixed in advance, sensitivity analyses and the reporting of negative results.

The University of Pannonia has launched the Human- and Society-Centered AI Research Network, the first multidisciplinary research community of the University’s Network of Research Excellence. Its 41 members come from the Faculties of Business and Economics, Engineering, Humanities and Information Technology, from the campuses in Veszprém, Zalaegerszeg and Nagykanizsa, and from outside the University.
The network asks how artificial intelligence transforms people’s cognition, identity, creativity and relationships, and how it changes collaboration, decision-making and adaptability in groups, organizations and social institutions. The levels are linked by one question: when does AI become help after which people can do more on their own – and when does the performance gain remain tied to the system?
Research is organized into nine connected lines, from cognitive partnership and creativity, organizational change and stakeholder impact, through AI risk and governance, trustworthy and explainable AI and human-centered industry, to AI in education, the AI-supported university and the AI capability of small and medium-sized enterprises. All studies share one framework, so that results from different settings can be compared.
The network works as an open, cross-faculty and self-organizing community. Members keep their home faculties and institutes and connect through shared questions, data and methods, joint publications and pilots. Researchers and doctoral candidates of the University and external researchers are welcome to join.
The founding workshop will take place on 11 December 2026.

title: The AI-Supported University and Institutional Decisions
text:
The problem
The name carries an organizational-psychology message: it is worth studying how the way an AI introduction is communicated affects people’s sense of control and willingness to participate – without assuming that wording alone causes acceptance or resistance. Management research describes the automation–augmentation paradox: the two strategies presuppose each other, and emphasizing either one alone has unfavorable consequences.
The university’s Strategic Planning and Analysis Centre supports data-informed decisions with data-science and AI tools. Research connected to it already covers educational and occupational networks, explainable turnover prediction in organizational networks, the analysis of student course-evaluation texts and the distribution-based assessment of research capacity. The relationship is mutual: real institutional questions and data on one side, methodological, ethical and impact-assessment expertise on the other.
Researching one’s own institution carries specific risks. Operational and research roles must be kept apart, ethics approval obtained in advance and negative results published. Participants are employees and students who depend on the institution, so participation is voluntary and without consequences, data are collected anonymously and, where possible, by people independent of the unit studied. No automatic personnel evaluation or ranking may be derived from the analyses.

The problem
Manufacturing makes the effects of AI on people measurable: workload, decision quality, trust and error risk in human–AI teams. Immersive and multimodal environments raise the question of how cognitive load, presence and user control mediate their effects.

title: AI in Education and Learning Support
text:
The problem
Unrestricted generative AI can improve performance during practice while reducing the knowledge learners later show on their own; tutors designed according to research-based pedagogical principles, by contrast, can produce larger learning gains. International frameworks distinguish students’ independent learning, joint use by teachers and students, and support for teachers’ work, and describe the AI competences of students and teachers in human-centered, ethical and pedagogical dimensions.
The psychological core of the line is self-regulated learning: goal setting, strategy use, self-monitoring and reflection. An AI tutor can support these – or take them over from the learner. The key question is therefore whether, after support, students plan and check their work more independently. Theory is the starting point; the effect of a tutor has to be shown in our own studies.
The EU AI Act classifies AI systems used for admission, for assessing learning outcomes, for steering learning and for monitoring exams as high-risk, and it prohibits emotion recognition in educational institutions. In our pilots the result can therefore never be an automatic decision about a student.

title: AI in Education and Learning Support

Under which design principles does AI strengthen learning rather than replace it (learning-support tutors; thinking first, help second; asking instead of explaining)?
How do assessment, academic integrity and authorship change, and which forms of assessment remain valid?
How can the AI literacy of university teachers and school teachers be developed, and how does it show up in actual teaching practice?
How do immersive, VR/AR-based AI assistants support learning, cognitive load and accessibility?
How can learning analytics help prevent dropout while people decide on interventions and students do not become automatic scores?

title: AI and Organizational Change
text:
The problem
The effect of introducing AI is mediated jointly by leadership goals, skills, incentives for knowledge sharing, psychological safety, perceived justice and processes. We study psychological safety not only as an outcome but as a possible precondition of learning together: do people dare to make mistakes, admit gaps in their knowledge or voice doubts about AI? This is not the same as general satisfaction or the absence of conflict.
The university itself is a natural field site: a cross-faculty knowledge base, AI-supported tools for managing relationships and tasks, inter-institutional knowledge sharing, reusable skills and joint workshops. We can observe how the density of the collaboration network, boundary-spanning ties, the reuse of shared knowledge items and the number of joint projects change.
The proposed design runs from an initial diagnosis through a jointly designed intervention, process and network measurement, interviews and surveys to follow-up. Pre-intervention trends, alternative explanations and data-protection conditions are documented, and the effects of the AI tool, of clarifying processes and of the joint workshops are separated. Participants’ own explanations can reveal whether a blockage stemmed from missing knowledge, diverging interests, lack of trust or overload.

title: AI and Organizational Change
text:
Research questions


Under which conditions does individual and group AI use become shared knowledge, organizational learning and lasting change in practice?
How do psychological safety and perceived justice shape whether people share knowledge – and their doubts about AI?
How do the division of labor, control and accountability shift as AI enters everyday work?
Can an AI-supported intervention measurably reduce silos between organizational units?

The problem
In persona-based impact assessment, personas curated by experts – and grounded in empirical data where possible – help to explore how an intervention affects different groups. A language model drafts a preliminary persona-level impact assessment, which human experts check, modify and document. Scores, uncertainty and decision triggers are organized into auditable evaluation records.
The research question is not only the accuracy of risk scoring: which stakeholder perspectives are missed, how robust the conclusions are to the choice of model and prompt, how the AI assessment relates to expert consensus, and whether the method improves the decisions of planners. An urban-development case study is the starting point; the approach can be carried over to public services, campus and workplace development, and to student recruitment and support, where the perspectives of prospective students, families and teachers differ widely.
At the level of society we follow digital inequalities and inclusion, access to education and services, social trust, stakeholder participation and contestability, the transformation of professions and employment, and the consequences for public services, regions and cities.

Research questions


How are the benefits, burdens and opportunities for influence of AI distributed across social groups?
Which stakeholder perspectives are missed in AI-supported decisions, and can persona-based assessment surface them?
How robust are AI-generated impact assessments to the choice of model and prompt, and how do they compare with expert consensus?
Which institutional and policy conditions support equitable access, participation and responsible use?

Testable hypotheses

H3 Persona-based risk discovery identifies more stakeholder impacts than a conventional, expert-only workshop – provided that the personas are empirically grounded.

Every hypothesis calls for an appropriate control, outcomes fixed in advance, sensitivity analysis and the reporting of negative results.
